data.title: Hacker gets data on millions of California students, state education department says
data.description:
The California Department of Education said on Friday a hacker accessed the data of millions of students, including names, birth dates, addresses and disability status, by exploiting the system of a non-profit contractor that works with the state.

The hacker accessed the data of "all students enrolled in the three previous school years," the department said. More than 5.7 million students were enrolled in California during the 2025-2026 school year, according to the department.

The non-profit, Educational Testing Service, on Friday began notifying students and their families of the breach, which was identified late last month but found to have been ongoing since May, the education department said.

The non-profit identified the breach involving a secure file transfer protocol site on September 25 and began an investigation, according to the California agency.

"The investigation determined that an unauthorized party used a compromised login credential to access the site and copy files containing California student information at various times between May 22 and September 18, 2026," the education department said.

Educational Testing Service has not found that any of the information has been made public so far, the education department said, adding that Social Security numbers and sensitive financial information were not accessed.

In an October 2 letter to county and district school officials, the California agency said the testing service had stopped "normal enrollment data processing."

"The CDE is actively working to minimize disruption and resume affected assessment activities in a timely manner," the department said.

In California, Educational Testing Service administers statewide assessments including those for English language proficiency.

"We have implemented additional safeguards, including enhanced monitoring, strengthened access controls, and further third-party review of our security practices," Educational Testing Service said in a statement to Reuters. "Our priority remains the students, families and educators we serve and safeguarding the assessment programs we deliver for our clients and partners globally."

data.title: Wall Street tumbles as worries about AI trade and high oil prices weigh
data.description:
Wall Street tumbled on Friday, with CoreWeave, Broadcom and other AI-related ​technology stocks under renewed pressure, while a jump in oil prices spooked traders heading into the weekend.

The Nasdaq was ‌on track for a loss of over 4% for the week, hammered by concerns that debt-laden AI infrastructure companies may not turn profits in time to repay debts, particularly with borrowing costs expected to rise.

Nvidia-backed CoreWeave slumped 12%, bringing its loss over the past five sessions to about 25%. The data center operator's ​bonds also sold off sharply this week, pushing yields above 15%.

Broadcom fell 3.6%, and the PHLX chip index sank 2.5%, ​on track for its eighth straight day of declines.

Investors on Friday were also watching oil prices jump more ⁠than 3% due to Middle East supply worries.

"There is some fear in the market," said Rob Haworth, senior investment strategist at U.S. ​Bank Wealth Management in Seattle. "High oil prices, in particular, tend to weigh on the price/earnings multiple of stocks, and so I think you have ​investors looking to be cautious into the weekend rather than take more risk."

Adding to concerns around AI financing, some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors are weighing a lower valuation for the company in its upcoming IPO, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

The S&P 500 was down 1.22% at 7,649.71 points.

The Nasdaq ​declined 2.19% to 26,128.13 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.55% at 51,891.77 points.

Six of the 11 S&P 500 ​sector indexes declined, led lower by communication services (.SPLRCL), opens new tab, down 2.52%, followed by a 2.38% loss in information technology.

The S&P 500 was set for its steepest weekly ‌loss since ⁠January, and the Nasdaq was heading for its sharpest weekly fall since June.

Third-quarter earnings season shifts into gear next week with reports from Tesla, Meta Platforms and Procter & Gamble. Analysts on average see quarterly earnings surging over 30%, driven by AI-related megacaps, according to LSEG data.

While the S&P 500 remains up about 12% in 2026, most of that gain has come from AI-related tech stocks, and the index’s median component ​has climbed only about 6%, year ​to date. About 185 S&P ⁠500 stocks have lost ground in 2026.

Hotter-than-expected consumer and producer inflation reports this week showed price pressures were extending beyond energy commodities.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh on Friday voiced optimism about US economic strength and surprise ​about how well global economies have been "hanging in there" during a lingering energy shock and tighter ​monetary policy to fight ⁠inflation.

Markets increasingly expect the Fed to keep interest rates unchanged this month. Barclays now expects 25-basis-point hikes each in December and January.

Tesla dropped 2.5% after the electric-vehicle maker unveiled a redesigned Roadster, powered by rocket-style thrusters, developed in collaboration with SpaceX.

Netflix appointed former Disney executive Peter Rice as chief content officer ⁠on Thursday. ​Its shares were down 2.9%.

Declining stocks outnumbered rising ones within the S&P 500 by ​a 1.3-to-one ratio.

The S&P 500 posted 19 new highs and one new low; the Nasdaq recorded 49 new highs and 263 new lows.

Trump threatens California officials with imprisonment over stance on mail ballots
data.description:
Key points:
  • Warnings come less than three weeks before US midterm elections
  • Justice Department suing to block state from counting ballots from alleged noncitizens
  • Voting by noncitizens remains uncommon, according to studies

By Jasper Ward

The US Justice Department on Friday warned Los Angeles County and California election officials they could be liable as abettors of a federal crime if they count mail ballots returned by more than 20,000 people the Trump administration says are probably noncitizens.

The warning to the Los Angeles County Assistant Counsel Peter Bollinger came less than three weeks before the November 3 midterm elections and days after the department gave California 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action. On Thursday, the Justice Department sued California to block the state from counting the ballots.

"Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful," Trent McCotter, the acting US deputy attorney general, wrote in a letter released on Friday. McCotter called on the county and California's secretary of state to reconsider their refusal to take steps that the Trump administration argues are needed to deter voter fraud.

US President Donald Trump shared the letter on Truth Social with the comment: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"

California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan were copied on McCotter's letter.

The county's counsel office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Weber's office referred Reuters to an earlier statement in which she said the Justice Department's attempts to "unlawfully gain access to states' protected ​voter data and purge voter rolls ⁠serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections."

An earlier letter that McCotter sent on Tuesday to Weber and Logan said the Justice Department provided officials in Los Angeles County with a "password-protected thumb drive" with the names of people ​the federal government "believes are likely noncitizens" that were sent mail-in ballots from California.

Los Angeles County Counsel Dawyn R. Harrison said on Thursday the county cannot comply with the Justice Department's requests because the Trump administration did not explain how the list was made. Friday's letter from McCotter said the Justice Department used "internal immigration records" and data matching.

In July, Trump said his administration had uncovered evidence of more than 275,000 non-citizens registered to vote, but it was not clear how many had actually voted.

In some previous cases, systems intended to verify citizenship have mistakenly flagged some naturalized US citizens as noncitizens. Studies have found that noncitizens casting actual ballots is exceedingly uncommon.

Since July, the Justice Department has ramped up prosecutions of people accused of illegally voting while not holding US citizenship. The White House has also pushed federal agencies to accelerate their review of at least 47 state voter rolls obtained by the Department of Homeland Security, according to an internal email seen by Reuters.

data.title: Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro pledges fiscal adjustment, rejects cuts to social spending
data.description:
Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro said on Friday that, if elected president, he would seek to curb Brazil's rising public debt without touching politically sensitive social spending commitments, rejecting media reports that his campaign was considering such measures.

The right-wing lawmaker, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, will face leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a runoff on October 25 and currently leads polls against the incumbent.

  • In an interview with TV Globo's Jornal Nacional, the most-watched newscast in Brazil, Bolsonaro pledged to deliver a 200 billion real ($39.49 billion) fiscal adjustment in the federal budget if elected

  • Bolsonaro dismissed proposals attributed by media reports to his campaign to halt real minimum wage increases, eliminate automatic adjustments for social benefits or reduce mandatory social expenditures

  • "There has been a lot of fake news circulating, and this is an important moment to set the record straight," the senator said

  • Instead, Bolsonaro said the adjustment would come from eliminating ministries, tackling mismanagement at state-controlled firms and monetizing federal real estate assets

  • Brazil's gross debt has risen more than 10 percentage points during Lula's term to 82.9% of GDP, while long-term interest rates have fallen since Bolsonaro's first-round victory

  • The senator also said he would not seek to reverse a constitutional amendment approved on Wednesday to shorten the working week in Brazil from six to five days

    ($1 = 5.0648 reais)

data.title: Hermès Is Targeting a New Emerging Market: The American Suburbs — WSJ
data.description:
By Natasha Khan

WILMETTE, ILL. — It used to be that if wealthy Americans wanted to buy Hermès, they made a pilgrimage to a store in Manhattan or Beverly Hills or a glamorous European city like Paris or Milan. Now, the brand is chasing customers by meeting them where they are: Short Hills, N.J., and Wilmette, Ill. The luxury-retail executives refer to such wealthy suburbs, as well as smaller American cities like Nashville, Tenn., and Austin, Texas, as "emerging markets."

The store in Wilmette, which opened in August and features a Spanish revival-style facade and dragonfly motifs, was built in an open-air mall across from a CVS pharmacy and down the road from a Jewel-Osco supermarket. Luxury neighbors Oscar de la Renta and Thom Browne recently opened up stores in the complex, too. Once Hermès moves in, other high-end tenants tend to follow.

The U.S. is emerging as a rare bright spot for luxury. Demand in traditional luxury strongholds like China and the Middle East has softened. In the first half of this year, the strongest region for sales growth for Hermès was in the Americas, where revenue grew at 15%. In another major market, Asia excluding Japan, the company's revenues grew by just 2%.

The luxury brand is one of the most valuable companies in the world. Its market cap has at certain points surpassed that of rival LVMH, despite being a single brand. But the headwinds of the industry are shifting.

The U.S. accounted for almost half of newly created millionaires in 2025, according to a June UBS report. That year, the country was home to 35.7% of the personal wealth in the world, ticking up from nearly 35% in 2024, UBS found in its analysis.

"Wealth in the U.S. today is widespread and diverse," said Diane Mahady, Hermès' chief executive for the Americas. "The data will show you that there are billionaires in 47 states."

The company, she said, sees "a lot of potential in the U.S. in terms of the number of stores." Hermès openings in the past few years include stores in Scottsdale, Ariz., and Princeton, N.J. It currently has 45 locations nationwide, including a new store in Manhasset on New York's Long Island opening this month.

Mahady recently presented a map at a meeting of global Hermès leaders that showed bubbles of wealth across America. "You know, the term 'emerging market' is probably a misnomer," she said. "You see that there's opportunity everywhere."

Physical retail has always been at the heart of Hermès strategy. Its 300 rarefied boutiques are where the high-end brand, known for its leather craftsmanship and status handbags, derives most of its sales. Hermès made about 16 billion euros, or $17.9 billion, in revenue last year.

The company opens only a few stores a year in part because Hermès typically has one Parisian architecture firm do the design and each shop has to be different from the stores that have come before it.

"Our strategy would boil down to the singularity of every location," Mahady said. "We don't want any two stores to be the same."

When the Hermès team decides where to build, a few factors come into play. They look at data demographics. They do a ZIP Code analysis of where existing clients live and where e-commerce clients seem clustered. They analyze shopping patterns and adjacency to other lifestyle destinations, for example a fantastic coffee shop or restaurant.

When Hermès opened in a redbrick former hosiery factory in Nashville last year, there was a Soho House and some popular eateries nearby, but not many other retail options.

"Businesses are moving their headquarters to Nashville, then their executive population also moves to Nashville, and we start to say, 'OK, this maybe can be a place where our clients are moving to or enjoying living there, and that can be a place for us,'" Mahady said.

For the location in Wilmette, the calculation was different. Hermès' downtown 6,000-square foot Chicago location was only a 35-minute drive away.

Executives were trying to solve a puzzle: They could see some clients in Chicago's affluent North Shore suburbs weren't buying from the downtown Chicago store. That store tended to attract customers from neighboring states like Wisconsin, Minnesota and Ohio.

Hermès executives theorized that North Shore shoppers might like having a store closer to them, the kind of place they could stop by while walking the dog or in between errands.

Now that the 4,400-square foot Wilmette store is open, Hermès executives see much more local clientele there.

Hermès employees are quick to bring up that theirs is a sixth-generation family business and artistic stewardship is part of the job: All of the company's leather handbags must be made in France by family decree, which in part explains the extraordinary bottleneck for their bags, including the Birkin, which can retail for well over $11,000.

But Hermès is trying to diversify. Leather goods and saddlery accounted for 44% of the brand's revenue in 2025. It is expanding clothing, silks and shoe offerings in an effort to draw more shoppers.

This summer, the brand hosted its first-ever major women's ready-to-wear runway show in Los Angeles.

Store directors occupy an important position in the effort to grow the customer base. Many have been with the company for decades, and lean on extensive personal relationships. Hermès moves talented salespeople around the country often and they are responsible for client outreach.

When store managers who work in close proximity — say, at the Chicago and Wilmette locations — go on their quarterly buying trips to Paris, they keep an eye on whether the inventory they choose overlaps.

"We're almost like a loose confederation of small specialty stores, and I think that creates such a rich culture for us," Mahady said.

Born in Horseheads, N.Y., Mahady got her first retail position in high school, with a part-time job at Tallman's Department Store in Painted Post, a New York second-generation family business specializing in big and tall and selling Carhartt, Red Wing and Dickies to factory workers in the foundry across the street.

She was hired by Saks after college and spent 12 years in various buying and planning roles, ultimately becoming a vice president in the men's sportswear division. She also worked for LVMH and Coach before joining Hermès in March of 2021.

Hermès didn't operate like other luxury retailers, Mahady realized. She had a lot more free rein to experiment with different sales models, without a need for a centralized directive or a one-size-fits all solution.

But it was crucial to get the store mix right. Stores needed to be distinct, but complement each other.

Each is decorated with photography and art pieces from the family collection, many of which are equestrian-themed. Each has to feel homey: Some clients end up dropping in for coffee or champagne several times a week, Mahady said.

And each has to blend into the community, said Pierre-Alexis Dumas, Hermès artistic director. It's an extension of an ethos championed by Dumas's father, Jean-Louis, who ran the company for close to three decades.

"He always told me we have to be American in America. We have to be Japanese in Japan," Dumas said at a recent opening of another store, in the Williamsburg neighborhood in New York's Brooklyn borough. "We have to engage in a dialogue. We cannot just come as conquerors."

Write to Natasha Khan at natasha.khan@wsj.com

data.title: PNB Q2 Net Profit Rises 13% To Rs 5,532 Cr, Gross NPA Ratio Falls To 2.55%
data.description:
Punjab National Bank’s net interest income rises 10 per cent year-on-year to Rs 11,601 crore in Q2 FY27, while the gross NPA ratio falls to 2.55 per cent

State-owned Punjab National Bank (PNB) reported a 13 per cent year-on-year rise in net profit to Rs 5,532 crore for the September quarter of FY27, supported by growth in net interest income and an improvement in asset quality. Profit was also higher than the Rs 5,253 crore recorded in the preceding quarter, while the bank’s gross non-performing asset (NPA) ratio declined to 2.55 per cent at the end of September.

Net interest income (NII), the difference between interest earned on loans and other assets and interest paid on deposits, increased 10 per cent to Rs 11,601 crore in the July-September quarter from Rs 10,517 crore a year earlier. On a sequential basis, NII rose 7 per cent from Rs 10,798 crore in the April-June quarter.

PNB’s gross NPA ratio fell by 90 basis points from 3.45 per cent in the year-ago quarter to 2.55 per cent in Q2 FY27. In absolute terms, gross NPAs declined to Rs 34,190 crore as of September 2026 from Rs 40,343 crore a year earlier, a reduction of Rs 6,153 crore.

The bank’s provision coverage ratio, which indicates the extent to which provisions cover bad loans, increased to 97.32 per cent from 96.01 per cent in the corresponding quarter last year. However, the slippage ratio, which tracks the pace at which loans turn into non-performing assets, rose to 0.77 per cent from 0.71 per cent.

PNB’s global business, comprising total deposits and advances, grew 12 per cent year-on-year to Rs 31.18 lakh crore in the September quarter, compared with Rs 27.86 lakh crore a year earlier. Global deposits rose 9.9 per cent to Rs 17.77 lakh crore from Rs 16.17 lakh crore over the same period.

The bank’s global net interest margin improved to 2.58 per cent from 2.50 per cent in Q2 FY26, while return on assets remained unchanged at 1.05 per cent.

As of September 2026, PNB had a nationwide network of 10,481 branches and 10,915 ATMs.

Shares of Punjab National Bank closed at Rs 116.30 on Friday, up 1 per cent from the previous close. The stock gained more than 1 per cent over the past month and delivered a 2 per cent return over the preceding six months.

data.title: NSC Clears Rs 1,194.92 Cr Investment For Five ITI Clusters Under PM-SETU
data.description:
India’s effort to bring industrial employers into vocational training has secured another round of investment, with five new plans worth Rs 1,194.92 crore approved under the Pradhan Mantri Skilling and Employability Transformation through Upgraded ITIs (PM-SETU) scheme.

The latest approvals take the cumulative investment cleared under the programme to Rs 3,687 crore. The projects involve five industry partners and cover Industrial Training Institute (ITI) clusters in Maharashtra, Odisha and Jammu and Kashmir.

The five partners are Tata Steel Foundation, BVG India, Belrise Industries, Eagle Infra India and Inderdeep Infra India. Their participation spans two clusters in Maharashtra, one in Odisha and two in Jammu and Kashmir.

Industry Takes Five Positions

BVG India, in consortium with BVG Foundation, will support the Pune cluster with an approved investment of Rs 241 crore. Belrise Industries will partner in the Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar cluster, where the investment plan stands at Rs 238.01 crore.

Tata Steel Foundation will work with the Kataka cluster in Odisha under a plan worth Rs 240.50 crore. The remaining projects cover Jammu, with Eagle Infra India as the partner and an investment of Rs 240 crore, and Srinagar, where Inderdeep Infra India will support a plan worth Rs 235.41 crore.

Together, the five plans account for Rs 1,194.92 crore. The National Steering Committee approved them at its meeting on 16 October 2026, chaired by Debashree Mukherjee, Secretary, Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship.

The Hub-And-Spoke Model

The projects will follow a hub-and-spoke structure. A central ITI will anchor each cluster and work with four associated institutes. The model is designed to coordinate upgrades across institutions rather than confine investment to a single campus.

The approved plans cover modernisation of training infrastructure, courses aligned with industry needs, trainer development and stronger employer participation. The programme also encourages clusters to pursue International Organization for Standardization (ISO) certification and include at least one WorldSkills-aligned trade or competency area in their implementation plans.

These measures place the focus on more than physical upgrades. The value of the investment will depend on whether institutes can deliver training that reflects the equipment, technical processes and competencies employers require.

Trainer Development Continues

The committee also reviewed progress under the scheme’s Training of Trainers programme. According to the ministry, 3,744 trainers had received training through National Skill Training Institutes as of October 2026.

The latest approvals follow a September round worth Rs 735.70 crore for ITI clusters in Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and Telangana. The additional plans broaden the scheme’s geographical reach and increase the investment approved so far.

data.title: RBI Approves Merger Of Emirates NBD’s India Branches With RBL Bank
data.description:
The three branches will become part of RBL Bank’s network from 1 December 2026, as part of Emirates NBD’s proposed USD 3 billion investment in the Indian lender

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has approved the merger of Dubai-based Emirates NBD Bank’s three Indian branches with RBL Bank, with the integration scheduled to take effect on 1 December 2026. The move is part of Emirates NBD’s proposed acquisition of a controlling stake in the Indian private sector lender.

In a notification dated 16 October the central bank said the merger had been sanctioned under Section 44A(4) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. Following the integration, Emirates NBD’s Indian branches will become part of RBL Bank’s domestic branch network.

The proposed transaction was announced in October 2025, when Emirates NBD outlined plans to acquire a 60 per cent stake in RBL Bank for approximately USD 3 billion. The agreement also provided for the consolidation of Emirates NBD’s existing banking operations in India with those of RBL Bank.

In January 2026, the Competition Commission of India (CCI) cleared the proposed transaction. The deal comprises a preferential allotment of shares that could give Emirates NBD up to 60 per cent of RBL Bank’s paid-up equity capital, an open offer for up to 26 per cent of its expanded voting capital, and the merger of the three Indian branches.

The RBI approved Emirates NBD’s proposal in April to acquire up to 74 per cent of RBL Bank’s share capital, subject to the condition that the Dubai-based lender maintain a minimum holding of 51 per cent. The central bank also restricted Emirates NBD’s voting rights in RBL Bank to 26 per cent.

On 15 May, RBL Bank said the regulatory and government approval process for the proposed investment had been completed. The transaction includes a primary capital infusion of approximately USD 3 billion (Rs 26,850 crore), which the bank described as one of the largest international investments in India’s banking sector.

With the RBI’s latest approval, the merger of the three Indian branches is scheduled to take effect on 1 December, completing another step in the integration of Emirates NBD’s Indian banking operations with RBL Bank.

data.title: Without Fibre, There Is No AI: STL CTO Badri Gomatam
data.description:
Sterlite Technologies CTO explains why optical networks are the unsung layer of AI infrastructure, how an eight-year-old R&D bet is now paying off, and why terahertz does not worry him

Ask most people what powers the AI boom, and they will say GPUs. Ask the people building data centres, and the answer includes something far less glamorous: the fibre that connects those GPUs to each other.

That is the space Sterlite Technologies (STL) occupies. The Pune-headquartered company is an optical and digital technology firm with more than 780 patents, serving data centre and cloud companies, telecom operators, internet service providers and large enterprises. In plain terms, STL makes the optical fibre, the cables and the connectivity products that carry data inside data centres, across cities and into homes. It does this as a vertically integrated manufacturer, producing everything from the glass preform to the finished cable.

The AI build-out has put that business in a strong position. STL reported record quarterly revenue of Rs 1,910 crore and a net profit of Rs 197 crore for Q1 FY27 on 24 July 2026. It raised Rs 1,500 crore through a qualified institutional placement in July. More recently, its subsidiary secured a long-term supply agreement with an international hyperscale partner, with a potential value of around USD 1.2 billion and allocations running from 2026 to 2030.

I met Dr Badri Gomatam, STL’s Chief Technology Officer, at India Mobile Congress 2026. We spoke about what that means for a fibre maker, how STL’s research bets are playing out, and where the technology goes next. I also picked his brain about the ongoing AI doomerism. Here are the edited excerpts:

The theme of India Mobile Congress 2026 is “Scaling Without Boundaries”. How is Sterlite Technologies doing that?

The conversation around AI has been all about GPUs and not so much about fibre. I think that has changed significantly in the last two to three years. Globally, there is a realisation that without the optical network, there is no AI. There is no inference and no training. You can see it in the demand versus supply: there is a limited supply of fibre and cable. People have slowly realised what it takes to build this product. What does it take to run a draw tower? What does it take to run a glass factory? That is one reason STL is a recognised name in AI infrastructure.

For us, scaling without boundaries has several dimensions. One is sheer capacity. We have announced huge investments over the last few weeks. The second is the investment in advanced technology. Last year we announced hyperscaler orders, and that is now moving towards a couple of billion dollars. These are very high-density products with record-setting fibre counts, and they are tough to make, tough to yield, and tough to manufacture. We are among the pioneers in this field.

We are also helping customers scale with new products. What we are showing here is our multicore fibre, which compresses four transmission cores into a single strand of glass. That changes the game in terms of deployment and time to market.

And on the R&D side?

We have been investing in multicore for several years, and we are driving the standards. My colleague over there is the vice chairman of Study Group 15 at the ITU. On top of that, we are investing in connectivity, such as pre-terminated assemblies that come with connectors, so you can hook up all these GPUs and racks very quickly. The connectivity business is a little new for us. Not totally new, but the scale at which we are doing it is.

Many of our readers and viewers are not into enterprise tech or AI infrastructure. How would you explain what Sterlite actually does?

At a base level, we are a vertically integrated manufacturer of fibre, cable and termination products. That is not hard to understand. You see it in your LAN cable and in your home broadband. What we do is hold the base technology layers. We synthesise the chemicals and raw materials in-house, we generate power in-house, and we build the glass preform, the fibre, and the cable in-house. So we make not just the end product but also the raw materials that go into it.

We are a fully vertically integrated, completely Indian-based supplier, and we hold the intellectual property, with about 780 patents. That R&D footprint gives us market strength. Whether the business goes to hyperscalers in North America, Western Europe, or elsewhere, it is a result of our core manufacturing strength, starting with our plants in India.

How has R&D at Sterlite evolved over the last few years, given how quickly the AI landscape has changed?

What is funny is that a product like multicore, which is all over the news today, is something we started eight years ago. There was a vision that this was going to happen. We ran pilots, trials, and proofs of concept, and slowly brought it to a point where a business was forming around it. These investments are incubated carefully over several years. They do not happen overnight.

Our rollable ribbon technology is similar. We have been supplying it for eight years, and we are one of the largest suppliers in the world. So when the big shift happened in the AI market, we were poised for it. It took us a few weeks or months to go from small cables to gigantic ones.

We work in platforms: a cabling platform, a fibre platform, and now a connectivity platform. All three are funded through corporate R&D. We were fortunate to be there at the right time, and a little luck is always required. But things were already working before the market hit us, and that helped us scale quickly.

In simple words, what does your hollow core fibre technology do, and how?

We spoke about it this year and made a couple of announcements. As a technology, though, it is at least 15 years old in terms of the science. What is new is that it has started showing excellent commercial potential for data centres.

The fibre works by trapping light in the centre of a nested arrangement of tubes, circles within circles. Think of it as a hall of mirrors. Light has nowhere to go but stay in the middle, so it cannot escape sideways and can only travel along the length of the fibre. That is a simple way to put it, and I am not doing it full justice. The hard part is manufacturing it. That was pioneered in the UK and has now spread worldwide, and there is a lot of uptake because the commercial benefits are clear.

Has this technology been rolled out in India yet?

I think we were the first to announce it in cable form. Pilots are commencing, and I expect deployments to begin in a year or two.

During a keynote at the IMC, an audio-visual presentation suggested that the future of communication may not involve fibre at all, pointing to terahertz transmission. Does that bother you?

I did not attend that session, so I cannot speak to exactly what was said. But what people forget is that fibre goes very long distances, at very low energy and at extremely low cost. Terahertz has its niche and its place. Like every technology, it has intrinsic limitations, and line of sight is one of the key ones. Fibre has its own limitation: you have to put it in the ground, which means infrastructure spending and civil works. But in terms of energy per bit, there is no better commercial option.

We are talking about transmitting terabits of data today. It will be difficult for a single physical layer to take that over. I do not think anyone said there will be no more fibre. Perhaps that is just how it came across.

So it does not worry you?

Not at all.

We are at the threshold of an era of autonomous agents doing work for us every day. How does that affect Sterlite, and your approach to things?

I am not the best person to comment on labour disruption from agents, and it is not something I worry about. For a manufacturer like us, the value of AI lies in efficiency and analysis. There is a great deal to be learnt from the data coming out of our production units, and that is where I see it helping most.

Follow BWTV Prime and BW Businessworld for all things tech.

Deep Majumdar

BW Reporters Deep Majumdar is a writer and video producer specializing in consumer technology, semiconductors and artificial intelligence. With a passion for uncovering the intricacies of modern tech, Deep's articles illuminate the evolving landscape of these fields. Beyond the written word, Deep extends his expertise to the visual realm as a producer for BWTV. His video productions cover a wide range of topics, including but not limited to personal technology and AI.

data.title: Jyothsana Vasudevan Takes Over As SRF’s President And CHRO
data.description:
The HR leader joins from Avaada Electro, bringing experience across manufacturing, employee relations, talent strategy and organisational transformation

SRF Limited has appointed Jyothsana Vasudevan as President and Chief Human Resources Officer (CHRO), bringing experience across strategic human resources leadership, organisational transformation, talent management, employee relations and capability development in manufacturing, energy and industrial businesses.

Vasudevan joins SRF from Avaada Electro, where she served as Senior Vice President – HR, Manufacturing, leading human resources for the company’s expanding solar manufacturing business. Her responsibilities spanned operations across Noida, Greater Noida, Dadri and Nagpur, with a focus on talent mobilisation, total rewards, employer branding, organisational culture and HR capability development.

Leadership Experience At Shell

Vasudevan spent a substantial part of her career at Shell, holding regional and global HR leadership roles. As Global Resourcing Manager for India, Malaysia, the Philippines and Poland, she led talent acquisition and capability-building initiatives across these markets.

During her tenure, she established a talent sourcing capability in Manila that contributed to an average external recruitment time-to-fill of 40 days. She also institutionalised the VISTA framework, which provided business leaders with external talent intelligence to support workforce planning, location strategy and build, borrow and buy decisions. Additionally, she redesigned global resourcing competency frameworks and introduced structured development approaches based on the 70-20-10 learning model.

She also served as Country Head – Employee Relations and Industrial Relations for India, overseeing the employee relations agenda across manufacturing facilities, corporate offices, fuel retail operations and lubricants businesses. Her work included strengthening workplace conduct and anti-harassment programmes, developing leadership capabilities in employee relations and establishing employee wellness initiatives.

Vasudevan designed and institutionalised India Wellness Month, bringing together more than 50 internal and external partners to support physical, mental and financial well-being. She also strengthened compliance governance across an employee base of approximately 10,000, introducing risk management frameworks and business-level compliance dashboards.

Regional And Business HR Roles

As HR Leader – Lubricants Supply Chain for Asia Pacific, the Middle East and Southern Africa, Vasudevan supported more than 1,100 employees across manufacturing plants, warehouses and corporate functions. Her responsibilities included regional integration, organisational redesign, leadership development and cultural transformation. Her work in embedding diversity and inclusion into business leadership practices earned her a Global Executive Vice President Award at Shell.

Her other roles at the company included Talent Manager – Downstream Businesses, Learning Manager – Global Functions, Learning Manager – Projects and Technology, and HR Manager – India Retail, Supply and Distribution. These assignments covered talent strategy, succession planning, learning transformation and organisational change.

Before Shell, Vasudevan worked at Whirlpool Corporation as Senior Manager – HR and Manager – Corporate HR. She supported HR business partnering for regional technology teams, talent acquisition, leadership development, employee engagement and employer branding.

Her initiatives contributed to a 50–60 per cent reduction in vacancy-filling time, employee attrition of 14 per cent against an industry benchmark of 25–30 per cent, and a 10-point improvement in employee engagement scores. She also supported campus recruitment and management trainee development programmes that became recognised practices across Whirlpool’s Asian operations.

Vasudevan has also undertaken a strategic advisory assignment with zeapl.ai, focusing on talent strategy, organisational culture and capability development. She holds an MBA in Human Resources Development from Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha University, Delhi.

At SRF, her experience spans global HR strategy, manufacturing HR, industrial relations, talent transformation, organisational development, leadership capability and culture building.

data.title: Nasdaq sell-off extends; Semiconductor ETF posts worst week in 18 months while Cboe VIX jumps
data.description:
Benchmark indices on Wall Street had another down day on Friday, October 16, as AI and semiconductor-linked stocks continued to see investor exits, while a rise in crude oil prices further soured sentiment.

The Dow Jones ended 175 points lower on Friday, outperforming its tech-heavy peers S&P 500 and Nasdaq, and also managing to post a weekly advance of 0.7%. The S&P 500 ended 1.1% lower, while the Nasdaq Composite declined 2.1%. The chip stocks-heavy Nasdaq 100 index ended the session with losses of 2.5%.

For the week, the Nasdaq ended 4% lower, marking its worst weekly drop since June. The S&P 500 also posted a 2% weekly loss. Fears of competition from China and the struggles over debt repayments of companies engaged in massive data center buildouts, dragged the VanEck Semiconductor ETF down 3% on Friday and 10% for the week, the most it has falling weekly since April 2025.

Chipmakers were down for the eighth straight day, their longest losing streak since 2008. Shares of AMD, Broadcom, Intel were down between 4% to 6% on Friday, while memory chip makers Sandisk, Western Digital and Seagate fell between 7% to 7.5% overnight. Oracle Corp. shed another 5% and is now nearing a 52-week low.

CoreWeave, the main trigger behind the recent sell-off, fell another 11% on Friday, taking its week-to-date loss to 25%. The company's total debt has now risen to $51 billion.

The sell-off seen on Wall Street has taken the market's fear gauge or the Cbox Volatility Index (VIX) past the mark of 22, for the first time since June, and market participants expect that to go much higher in the near-term.

Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, continues to believe that the AI benefits will soon outweigh the concerns of investors.

"It’s going to be transformative. It’s going to impact in a very positive way every single industry and every single country. There’s no question it will continue, and we’re at the beginning of that," Huang told Bloomberg during an interview in Berlin.

Analysts suggest that the market debate has shifted from not just how large AI can become, but how large an investment will be needed further to realize the ultimate goal of becoming profitable.

Cathie Wood of ARK Investment Management, compared CoreWeave to Coinbase, whose bonds had also come under pressure initially but the company benefitted from the growth of the crypto industry in the long run. For CoreWeave, she believes that investing in the company will payoff as the fund also added the stock during this week's rout.

Another reason why sentiments were soured on Wall Street was the sharp jump seen in crude oil prices, where Brent jumped to $110 a barrel overnight as Iran escalated attacks in the Strait of Hormuz while Ukraine and Russia continued to attack each other's energy infrastructure, triggering further supply concerns.

(With Inputs From Agencies)

data.title: White House Press Secretary Is Out One Week After Being Named to the Role — WSJ
data.description:
By Brian Schwartz, Marianne LeVine and Melissa Korn

WASHINGTON — Katie Zacharia is out as White House press secretary, according to people familiar with the matter, just a week after President Trump announced her appointment to the high-profile role.

On Friday, Trump said he had suggested that Zacharia consider leaving the job. "I said, 'Is this for you Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this,'" Trump told reporters, adding that she had been treated "very rough" by the media.

The president said he spoke to Zacharia earlier on Friday, just before his comments to reporters as he left the White House for a rally in Georgia. He said he counseled her, "Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider."

A White House official and person familiar with the matter confirmed that she was being transitioned out of the job and wouldn't be returning as press secretary. Zacharia will be transitioning to a new role that will be announced at a later date, a person familiar with the plans said.

It caps a brief, chaotic run for Zacharia as the administration's chief spokeswoman. Trump announced her appointment last Friday, and her first day on the job was Monday. She quickly came under scrutiny after a shaky debut press briefing Tuesday, and faced questions about her claims that she was a lawyer.

"President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man," Zacharia posted on X Friday night. "It was an honor to work for him."

Zacharia, who was named to succeed Trump's previous White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, came into the role with little experience in government communications, although she frequently appeared as a commentator on cable news, catching the president's eye.

The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that even though Zacharia repeatedly referred to herself as a lawyer, and Trump called her an attorney in announcing her appointment, she didn't pass the bar exam when she took it in California in 2011 and isn't licensed in the U.S.

Zacharia said in an interview on Fox News's "Fox & Friends" on Friday that she wasn't asked whether she had passed the bar before she accepted the role. A White House official said Zacharia wasn't hired by the president to work on legal matters.

During her debut at the White House podium on Tuesday, Zacharia spoke in a stilted cadence while reading out a list of Trump's accomplishments and discussing her excitement for the job. She looked down at her notes rather than at the camera, repeated words and paused to find her place.

Zacharia also faced tough questions Thursday evening about her performance in the briefing room and her professional background on Fox News's "Hannity." Trump told reporters Friday that he had seen her appearances on both Fox News shows.

Sean Hannity pressed Zacharia on whether she took the bar again and asked her about her promotion of social-media posts identifying her as an attorney. Zacharia said those were retweets and that she had "corrected the record" to clarify that she wasn't endorsing the title.

"Why get into this long, drawn-out definition?" he asked, noting that most people don't see a difference between the terms lawyer and attorney. She replied that she had sought guidance on the appropriate label and wasn't being paid for legal advice, just analysis, when she appeared as a commentator and in other settings.

Zacharia was asked on "Fox & Friends" Friday morning whether she still had the president's confidence. She replied: "I'm standing here and I was able to travel with him through all of the midterm convention — or, excuse me, the midterm rallies, and I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me."

Fox News parent Fox Corp. and The Wall Street Journal's parent, News Corp, share common ownership.

Before taking the White House job, Zacharia served as a communications adviser to Trump Media & Technology Group, which operates the Truth Social platform. She also briefly worked at the Department of Homeland Security earlier in Trump's second term, and has appeared as a guest on media outlets including CNN, Fox News and Newsmax.

Current White House officials watching the initial briefing from their offices on Tuesday picked up on what they described as nervous energy coming from the podium and wondered why Zacharia held a briefing so soon after accepting the job, instead of taking more time to prepare. Current and former administration officials traded assessments of the performance on a group chat.

Zacharia spoke about the turnout at a recent Trump rally, as well as new jobs and border security, then took questions from reporters at Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail. The briefing lasted less than 15 minutes. At one point while speaking about her family, she mentioned "my president" — then corrected herself to say "my husband," joking about the flub.

Zacharia is expected to have dinner with Vice President JD Vance and his family at his residence Friday evening, a person familiar with the matter said.

Trump's leadership team saw significant turnover during his first administration, though that had calmed during his second stint in the White House. Sean Spicer, the first White House press secretary during Trump's first administration, was in the role for 182 days. Leavitt held the job for more than a year and a half.

Anthony Scaramucci served just 10 days as White House communications director in 2017. He addressed Zacharia in a post on X on Friday afternoon. "Dear @katiezacharia - speaking as the world's leading expert on short White House tenures: turn off the news and go enjoy your family. In time you'll realize that the Universe did you a major favor."

Write to Brian Schwartz at brian.schwartz@wsj.com, Marianne LeVine at marianne.levine@wsj.com and Melissa Korn at Melissa.Korn@wsj.com

data.title: Spending Boom Will Help Asia, India, Europe — Barron's
data.description:
India, Japan, and Poland are just some of the markets that will benefit from greater spending and investment around the world.

By Reshma Kapadia

There has been a regime change in the global economy and investment world, says Henry McVey, head of global macro and asset allocation at KKR, the alternative asset manager. If ultralow interest rates and consumer spending marked the prior regime, a higher inflation rate and global fixed-investment boom will shape the worlds of business and finance in the coming years. That boom extends far beyond artificial intelligence, he notes, to encompass spending on national security, energy, supply-chain resilience, and more.

McVey, formerly chief U.S. investment strategist at Morgan Stanley, sees ample investment opportunities as countries spend to fortify power grids, shore up supply chains, and reshuffle trade routes. After traveling to Europe and Asia in recent weeks, he says he is even more bullish than before, and thinks this investment cycle is broader, more durable, and likely more inflationary than he originally envisioned.

McVey is also chief investment officer of KKR's $34 billion-in-book-value balance sheet, used to seed new businesses and make strategic acquisitions. He recently spoke with Barron's about the implications of greater spending and investment for various markets and regions around the world. While most of KKR's investments are focused in private markets, McVey highlighted public and private-equity investments that stand to benefit.

An edited version of the conversation follows.

Barron's: Is there an investment trend that the market has underestimated?

Henry McVey: We are in a fixed-asset investment boom. The headline attention is on AI, but it is broader than that. It involves the reconfiguration of supply chains, national security initiatives, and a fundamental reconstruction of the energy system. All four pillars are driving stronger incremental growth than what we have traditionally seen.

We were living in a world of tight fiscal and loose monetary policy, and low inflation. Central banks overreached via quantitative easing to stimulate leverage, which ultimately led to consumption. The current model is predicated on faster growth in nominal gross domestic product and profits. Deregulation, tax incentives, and bigger growth opportunities are leading to more fixed investment, including more broad-based capex [capital expenditure] in the corporate sector. It is almost the exact opposite of the prior two decades, and the investment community understands that — but not the magnitude of the implications.

What are the implications?

The most interesting point is in Asia. Sixty percent to 75% of capex in the region isn't related to AI. The defense industry is growing, intra-Asia trade is booming, and the need for more power in new spaces is underappreciated. The story for Asia is up and to the right.

One of the more important structural trends across Asia is the continued deepening of trade within the region. Intra-Asia trade increased from 46% of total regional trade in 1990 to 60% in 2024, and we expect that share to reach approximately 68% by 2030. This shift reflects increasingly integrated supply chains, greater regional investment, and importantly, the emergence of Asian economies as larger end markets for one another.

This trend has further to run, creating opportunities in manufacturing, logistics, infrastructure, and businesses benefiting from rising regional consumption.

What other themes are attractive in Asia?

Corporate reform and corporate carve-outs is a megatheme in Japan, Korea, and increasingly in Singapore, which are must-own investment opportunities. For example, 40% of Japan's stock market — and 70% of Korea's — trades below book value, 17% of assets are in cash, and real interest rates are negative. This is an incredibly compelling backdrop for private-equity investors.

There is also a consumption upgrade theme. Indian executives are seeing the middle- to upper-income consumer increasing spending and the lower-income consumer retrenching. It is the same story I heard in London and in the U.S. The bifurcation creates opportunity as many consumers upgrade their spending.

What are some examples?

Nominal GDP in India is growing faster than anyplace else, so that creates attractive opportunities for investments in hospitals, education, and retirement security. In China, the main theme is value for money, much like what happened in the U.S. after the 2007 downturn. South Korea and Japan are more mature societies, welcoming AI because automation and digitization help with demographic challenges.

In Japan, we have invested in PHC Holdings [ticker: 6523.Japan], a diabetes-management products company that helps address the growing need for chronic-disease management in aging populations. Another investment is [privately held] Logisteed, which uses robotics, automated warehousing, and digital logistics systems to reduce dependence on manual labor. That helps companies respond to Japan's aging workforce and labor shortages.

How do you account for currency moves?

Currencies in Asia are generally undervalued, creating another tailwind for the region. Interest rates have been the focus for investors. For the next chapter, currencies are more front and center. Currencies respond to interest-rate moves and fiscal imbalances, and it seems we are in that world. The decision to hedge against currency swings will grow in importance.

What do higher interest rates mean for investors?

Inflation is at a higher resting heart rate than in the past. That means nominal GDP will be higher. You aren't going to get access to the low rates of the past, so you have to grow your way through this with productivity. That is where we are laser-focused at KKR. The ability to have a moat around your business and leverage technology and employee ownership, which keeps everyone rowing in the same direction, generates outsize results.

What does this new regime mean for the traditional 60% stocks, 40% bonds investment portfolio?

We have been advocating against government bonds for years, saying that the traditional correlation between stocks and bonds would go from negative to neutral or positive, preventing bonds from remaining a shock absorber in a portfolio. In the regime change I'm talking about, government debt is your Achilles' heel. Investors were probably overpricing the value of the risk-free rate.

I want to own more investments that aren't correlated to the stock market because the market has become increasingly concentrated. That would include more real assets, particularly infrastructure, in which most clients are underweight. Governments are levered and don't have excess free cash flow to fund all the fixed investment, so we are seeing spinoffs of transmission lines and roads — for example, in India. There, we own Highway Concessions One, a toll-road and transportation infrastructure company, and India Grid Trust, a publicly listed infrastructure trust focused on electricity transmission.

Tactically, publicly traded corporate bonds with three to four years of duration look interesting now in most parts of the world. Investors have priced in too many central bank interest-rate hikes. As rates normalize and investors realize that central bankers are just taking away emergency rate cuts made in 2025 and not embarking on a massive tightening cycle as in 1994 or 2021, liquid credit looks like an interesting near-term opportunity. Shorter-term high-yield debt is a key focus.

What risks are you monitoring most closely?

I am focused on semiconductor pricing. The semiconductor business is highly cyclical. Right now companies have strong margins, but that may not always be the case. I am also monitoring the cash flow of the large language models. We estimate 40% of the hyperscalers' order book is coming from LLMs, so they need to deliver on their business proposition.

Another concern is budget deficits in France — and in the U.S. and more mature Asian markets, where there are questions about what is the "right" government debt load. We think it is closer to 150% of GDP for developed economies, not 100% [where many debt/GDP ratios sit now]. One variable that could alter my regime-change framework would be a government shift toward tighter fiscal spending.

Could that happen in the coming months after elections in France or elsewhere?

AI, national security, defense, and supply-chain reconfiguration are largely existential threats. Both the public and private sector are going to spend around them for that reason.

There could be a tactical shift, but I don't think we will have a seismic change in government policies until the fixed-investment buildout is further along. That is why our portfolio is predicated on having the ability to withstand heightened geopolitical tensions, bigger deficits, a messy energy transition, and more supply-side shocks than in the past. We are looking to build portfolios that not only defuse those concerns but also position investors to benefit from the tailwinds.

China is quickly adopting AI. What are the implications?

AI is pervasive across sectors in China. There is a thirst to embrace AI in the healthcare and consumer sectors. That should be a sign of what's coming.

Our thesis on productivity was predicated on automation, digitization, and machine learning coming out of the Covid pandemic, not AI. So far, AI may have contributed a tenth to a hundredth of the increase we saw in productivity from 1% in the past decade to 2.4% in the past eight quarters. To understand how AI drives that next leg of productivity, you need to look beyond U.S. firms.

It is borderline irresponsible to not understand China's technology effort, even if you are going to buy the Magnificent Seven stocks. China is making significant inroads in open-source and low-cost models. One part of the world may demand the Maserati of AI, and another a regular car that is fast but a cheaper alternative.

While China has developed globally competitive industrial businesses, translating that competitiveness into stronger corporate profitability and returns on capital remains a challenge. By comparison, Japan and Korea offer more visible opportunities [for investors] from corporate governance reform, shareholder returns, and operational improvement.

Where else are you finding opportunity?

When we survey CEOs of the companies we are invested in, the No. 1 term they use is resiliency. We call this the "security of everything." Post-tariffs, post-Covid, post-wars, they want to make sure their supply chains work. One of the biggest impediments is consistency of power. The opportunity in power storage is probably underappreciated. We have also been investing in the providers to the energy providers.

Additionally, we have invested in vocational training, with stakes in companies such as Lightcast, a labor-market analytics business that helps employers and educational institutions identify skills gaps and better align workforce training with labor market needs. We need more plumbers, welders, and shipbuilders. Goods jobs surpassed services jobs in August, which hasn't happened for years.

Also, Europe is getting a huge bump in intra-Europe trade. Germany is exporting less to China and more to Eastern Europe. Poland is a notable beneficiary of the shift toward more-regional European supply chains, particularly in automotive manufacturing, industrial components, and logistics. Its proximity to Germany, established manufacturing capabilities, and integration into European trade networks make it an attractive location for companies seeking to regionalize production.

Thanks, Henry.

data.title: Market View — Barron's
Is This the Future of U.S. Tax Policy? Stay Tuned. — Barron's
data.description:
Voters in more than a dozen states are considering tax-related amendments in November.

By Joe Light

The ballot box in November won't just determine control of Congress. It could also provide a crystal ball for the future of U.S. tax policy — and whether early attempts to increase taxes on the wealthy in a handful of states becomes a national movement.

Voters in more than a dozen states are considering tax-related amendments to local laws or their state constitutions in November. But the eyes of many Democratic lawmakers are turned toward California, Washington, and Colorado, where voters are considering whether states can refill their coffers with levies specifically targeting millionaires and billionaires.

The outcomes will probably have an impact on how Democrats act the next time they have control of the White House and Congress. The last time Democrats had such control, under President Joe Biden in 2021, lawmakers moved forward with limited tax hikes. However, more-aggressive proposals to target the wealthy never made it past the whiteboard stage. If taxes on millionaires have strong victories in blue states this year, such proposals would have a much better shot next time, some analysts say.

"Whatever happens will probably be seen as a bellwether for progressive tax ideas across the whole country," says Bloomberg Intelligence tax analyst Andrew Silverman, of the California vote. "If it wins, supporters of a federal wealth tax will be energized. If it loses, detractors will use that loss to say that Americans don't want a tax on the wealthy."

The measures are in part a backlash to President Donald Trump's massive tax and spending bill that passed last year. That bill lowered taxes for most Americans, including the wealthy — and at the same time put stress on state budgets by pushing some costs of social safety net programs like food stamps and Medicaid onto local governments.

To protect their budgets, some legislatures decoupled their own tax law from federal law, essentially making companies or individuals calculate their taxable income differently than they do for the federal government. Some states, though, also went on the hunt for revenue elsewhere and settled on high-income earners and the ultrawealthy as the most politically palatable targets.

Advocates in favor of higher taxes on the wealthy say that voters' perceptions have been trending in their favor.

"It definitely is a growing trend nationwide. We're seeing more and more communities all across the country in every state looking toward progressive taxes as a way to address affordability concerns," says Amber Wallin, executive director of the State Revenue Alliance and the Alliance Action Fund, which advocate for progressive tax reform.

As evidence, Wallin points to Missouri, a state that Trump won by more than 18 percentage points in 2024. Voters there in August were asked to approve an amendment that would have phased out its income tax in favor of expanded sales taxes, but rejected it with 83% of the vote.

The efforts to raise taxes have gotten an assist from other states that approved taxes targeted to millionaires in the past and haven't seen some of the negative impact that had been predicted. New Jersey passed a tax hike on those making more than $500,000 in 2004, followed by California on income over $1 million.

Opponents of the increases in those localities said they would cause millionaires to leave for neighboring states. Though some did move, by and large the migration never materialized, says Cristobal Young, a sociology professor at Cornell University who studied the issue.

"Sure, people move sometimes, but migration rates are very low for high-income earners, and there's very little responsiveness to seeing their taxes change," Young says.

On the other side of the ledger, some Republican-leaning, or more moderate, states are considering measures to cut taxes further. In North Carolina, for example, voters are considering a provision to lower the cap on state income taxes to 3.5% from 7%. Florida is considering increasing its homestead exemption for property taxes to $250,000 from $50,000.

Emboldening the higher-tax advocates are polls showing that an overwhelming majority of Americans support higher taxes on the wealthy across party lines. About 61% of voters in September in a Wall Street Journal poll said that they support implementing a federal tax on Americans with a net worth of over $1 billion. About 66% said they'd favor raising the federal income tax for people who make more than $1 million a year.

The broadening support and the ballot measures' outcomes could be a preview of the tough decisions facing Congress, not just next year but also after the next president takes office in 2029. Lawmakers such as Sen. Bernie Sanders (I., Vt.), Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D., Mass.), and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D., N.Y.) have long called for higher taxes on the wealthy to help lower the deficit and pay for social programs.

Biden at various times proposed his own versions of a federal billionaire or millionaire tax, but even with unified control of Congress in 2021, Democrats didn't move forward with them. Biden's signature bill, the Inflation Reduction Act, established a minimum tax on corporations and a levy on stock buybacks, but Biden proposals to create a billionaire minimum income tax or raise marginal rates on high earners never made it into law.

Democrats' failure to raise taxes on the wealthy during the Biden administration makes some analysts skeptical that they could succeed in doing so next time they have control, even if the ballot measures pass.

"Once you have to have a vote on raising taxes, it's very difficult for a politician to do that. A lot of voters, even if the tax isn't targeted at them, are worried who's going to be next," says Stifel Chief Washington Policy Strategist Brian Gardner.

Opponents of the California tax, in particular, say it's poorly designed and potentially unconstitutional. The tax would impose a one-time 5% levy on the wealth of state residents with more than $1 billion in assets. Its opponents include not just billionaires but also Democrats such as Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Rep. Katie Porter (D., Calif.), who say it's poorly drafted.

Adding to the muddle is that in addition to the proposal for the one-time wealth tax in California, there are two other proposals that would prevent it from taking effect. Confusingly, a September poll from the Public Policy Institute of California showed a slight majority of likely voters supporting all three measures. Under California law, if conflicting ballot measures pass, the one with the most votes generally supersedes the other.

The Colorado and Washington state measures are more straightforward. In Colorado, voters are deciding whether to move from a flat state tax of 4.4% to a graduated structure with a top rate of 8.4%. Washington voters are deciding whether to repeal a 9.9% tax on households earning more than $1 million that passed the state legislature in March.

Broad taxes on the wealthy will be on the table if Democrats win a trifecta in 2028, but up until now lawmakers have focused more on vanilla tax-raising measures that have already garnered broad support in the party, says Silverman. Perennial targets include carried interest earnings for asset managers and corporate income-tax changes.

"Taxes on the wealthy are being proposed by Democrats, too, but they're swamped by more-traditional tax proposals," Silverman says.

data.title: Europe-China Trade Truce Helps Auto Makers — Barron's
data.description:
By Craig Mellow

A funny thing happened when European Union Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic went to Beijing a week ago. He came back with a concession.

Chinese counterparts agreed to limit hybrid vehicle exports, which have quadrupled over the past 18 months as an end-run around EU tariffs on all-electric cars. That won't automatically rescue Europe's floundering auto makers, much less close the yawning bilateral trade gap. Shares in Volkswagen, BMW, and Mercedes-Benz Group, all down by a third or more this year, barely reacted.

Nevertheless, "the fact that they got anything is a success after years of the Chinese being totally dismissive," says Andrew Small, director of the Asia program at the European Council on Foreign Relations.

The EU's goods trade deficit with China has more than doubled since prepandemic days and could hit a record 400 billion euros ($445 billion) this year. European leaders are increasingly fed up with China's penchant for keeping unprofitable companies alive, then selling their excess production at minimal margins abroad.

French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz posted a joint letter to the European Commission on Oct. 5, calling for a "credible instrument up to and including exclusion from the single market" for unnamed trade distorters. The imprimatur of Germany, Europe's top economy and leading China trade dove in recent years, marks a milestone, says Dimitar Lilkov, senior research officer at the Wilfried Martens Centre for European Studies.

Next steps remain unclear. Car imports are a symbolically resonant and easily defined target. In euro terms, though, Europe buys 10 times as much Chinese electrical equipment and seven times as much machinery as vehicles. "An approach to these more amorphous and bigger areas has to be invented," Small observes.

The good news for auto makers is they are using the tariff reprieve to fight back, says industry analyst Matthias Schmidt. Chinese EV sales are "plateauing" at about 15% of that category as VW and French competitor Peugeot roll out hot-selling new models. EVs will exceed 25% of new EU car sales this year, with a boost from Iran war-fueled petrol prices, he estimates.

The bad news is that European car manufacturers won't make much money. Chinese rivals at the gate plus the economics of EVs, where batteries account for much of the cost, are slashing margins from high-single digits to 3% to 4%, Schmidt reckons.

That leaves axing costs the key to survival. Investors were unimpressed this summer by VW CEO Oliver Blume's taboo-smashing plan to cut up to 100,000 jobs and close four German factories, notes Michael Field, European equity strategist at Morningstar. "VW is getting huge pushback from their unions and local governments," he says. "It's hard to square that circle."

VW shares are trading 80% below a theoretical fair value after crashing by three-quarters over the past five years, Morningstar estimates. Mercedes' upside is 50%. Field sees "no single short-term catalyst" to reverse dismal market sentiment, however.

Brussels' would-be tougher stance on China is constrained by at least two factors. One is the U.S., where Trump administration tariffs reduced EU exports by 16% in the first eight months of 2026. The second is Europe's commitment to slashing its carbon output, which depends largely on Chinese equipment.

"The European Green Deal has caused a huge wealth transfer to China," Lilkov comments.

Doing nothing is increasingly not an option, though.

data.title: Dividends Are Drying Up. How to Fight Back. — Barron's
data.description:
The dividend yield for the S&P 500 is paltry, at just over 1%. Here's how to tweak your investment strategy in response.

By Avi Salzman

John Rockefeller was a glum guy. He didn't drink alcohol, dance, or play cards. But there was one thing that put a smile on his face. "Do you know the only thing that gives me pleasure? It's to see my dividends coming in," he was quoted as saying back in 1908.

By that measure, Rockefeller would be positively distraught today. The S&P 500's dividend yield hit a record low of 1.07% for the second quarter. For investors who like to clip their coupons, there isn't much left to clip.

Measured on a daily basis, the yield is currently at 1.09%, just above its record daily low of 1.01%, which it hit on Sept. 1, 2000. The yield's decline that year ended up being a red flag. Within six months, the index had lost 17% of its value in the dot-com bust.

Today, the market looks healthier than it did in 2000, but many of the same dynamics are in place. Tech stocks with low or nonexistent dividends are leading the market, while dividend-paying stocks have been left behind.

Some longtime dividend-payers have also gotten stingier with their payouts. Target, for instance, hiked its dividend by 32% in 2021 and 20% in 2022. This year and last, it increased the dividend by just 1.8%. S&P 500 companies paid out the lowest dividends on record as a percentage of earnings in the second quarter, returning just 24.7% to investors, according to Sam Stovall, chief investment strategist at CFRA Research.

When times are good, like they have been over the past four years, it's easy to overlook the dividend yield. The S&P 500 has enjoyed double-digit percentage gains every year since 2023, so it hasn't mattered much to investors whether they get a 1% or 3% dividend yield on top of that.

But when the market goes through rockier stretches, or stocks are just doing OK, dividends are often the one bright spot in a portfolio. Historically, dividends have contributed 31% of the S&P 500's total return, according to S&P Dow Jones Indices, based on data from 1926 through February 2025. In the first decade of the 2000s, which ended with a fizzle, dividends contributed 68% of the total return.

By comparison, dividends barely make a blip in total returns today. In 2025, the market rose 16.4%. Adding dividends brought the total return to 17.9%.

One of the market's foremost dividend proponents now says investors can no longer rely on dividends alone as ballast for their portfolios. Jeremy Siegel, a professor emeritus at Wharton and the chief economist at investment firm WisdomTree Investments, had found that reinvested dividends accounted for 97% of real return for stocks between 1871 and 2003. Now he thinks investors need to take a wider view.

"Basing a strategy on dividends alone today is too narrow. That's why I recommend looking at shareholder return, which is buybacks plus dividends," he said in an interview. Before the 1980s, buybacks were rare, because they were viewed as a kind of market manipulation. Companies spent 10 times as much on dividends as buybacks in 1970, according to Morgan Stanley. But a rule change in 1982 offered companies legal protection for their buybacks, and the practice took off. By 2004, they were spending 1.3 times as much on buybacks as on dividends. Since then, companies have consistently spent more on buybacks than on dividends, excluding during recessions, Siegel found. This year, companies in the S&P 500 are set to pay out $827 billion in dividends, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. Goldman Sachs estimates they'll spend $1.4 trillion on buybacks.

Siegel says companies are responding to investor demands by shifting their shareholder return strategies toward buybacks, which are more tax-efficient for many investors. Investors have to pay taxes on their dividends, even if the dividends are simply reinvested back into the stock or index. And the wealthiest investors, who hold the majority of stocks, are taxed at higher rates on certain dividends than on their capital gains from selling stocks.

For those in the top income bracket, nonqualified dividends — payouts on stocks that were held for less than 60 days — are taxed as income at levels as high as 37%. Capital-gains rates and taxes on qualified dividends are capped at 20%. Siegel has advocated for tax policies that make dividends more appealing by eliminating taxes on dividends that are reinvested. But that proposal hasn't been adopted.

While buybacks may have tax advantages, they are seen as less dependable. They come and go based on the whims of management, unlike dividends, which companies will generally maintain unless something is going terribly wrong.

"While buybacks and dividends are arguably interchangeable, management teams commonly view buybacks as discretionary and dividends as sacrosanct," writes Michael Mauboussin of Morgan Stanley.

That makes dividends a particularly good sign of a company's health at a time when companies have gotten better at promoting metrics that can hide the underlying strength of their numbers. Separately, the discretionary nature of buybacks means there is a risk that companies increase their buyback programs at exactly the wrong times, increasing purchases when their shares are pricey and reducing them when they are undervalued. A 2011 study by McKinsey found that most companies ramped up repurchases when shares were on the way up, and cut back when the share price dropped.

Beyond the rise of buybacks, another reason that dividends have fallen out of favor is that companies are using more of their cash to grow. Exhibit A in this trend are the "hyperscaler" tech companies like Amazon.com, which have been spending so much to build out artificial-intelligence capabilities that there's often little money left for other priorities. Amazon recorded negative free cash flow in its latest quarter, along with other big tech names like Alphabet and Oracle. "Capital spending in support of AI is being rewarded more than a company raising its dividend," says Todd Rosenbluth, head of research at index provider VettaFi.

The good news for yield-seeking investors is that bonds are now a much more attractive source of income, with 10-year U.S. Treasury notes now yielding 5.2% — a full percentage point more than at the start of the year.

Meanwhile, financial innovations are offering new ways to derive income from equities. From the start of 2026 through September, investors poured $52 billion into derivative income exchange-traded funds such as the JPMorgan Equity Premium Income ETF, which try to enhance income gains from stock ownership by using options contracts.

That eclipses the $46 billion of net inflows into dividend ETFs, according to VettaFi. Among those traditional ETFs, the most popular is Vanguard Dividend Appreciation, which owns companies that have consistently raised their dividends. But its yield remains measly, at just 1.5%. An alternative is the Schwab US Dividend Equity ETF, which yields 3.3%.

Todd Trubey, a senior analyst for equity strategies at Morningstar, likes the Vanguard High Dividend Yield ETF. Its 2.4% yield isn't spectacular, but the fund's 0.04% expense ratio is hard to beat. A more expensive but higher-yielding option that he likes is the BNY Mellon Enhanced Dividend and Income ETF, which holds stocks and preferred shares. It yields 7.5%, with a 0.5% expense ratio.

It's also worth looking overseas, where many companies continue to pay fat dividends. The iShares International Select Dividend ETF yields 4.8%, and charges 0.5% in expenses. It holds a mix of energy, tobacco, and telecom stocks, among others.

Trubey says that retirees who like to live off quarterly payouts find the dearth of dividends particularly tricky. "At the end of the day, you don't need dividends," he says. "You also don't need the yield from bonds in order to retire. You can always just sell a little bit of your portfolio now and again. It's just that people don't like to do that. We're used to getting paychecks, and dividends correspond to those."

The market environment has clearly changed. In order to adjust, investors may have to think a little less like employees, and a little more like owners.
